Same decimal-vs-percent ambiguity as the bronze/silver ratio steps, just appearing in a check line late in the walk rather than the main path.

findings.step: Rough check: 5 ÷ 25 × 100 =
findings.why: This is a ×100 computation in the same form as the graded answer two steps above (5 ÷ 24 × 100, to 1 decimal place = 20.8, which IS labelled %), but this box carries no % label — the inconsistency could make a student unsure whether to write 20 or 0.2.
findings.fix: Label the box '%' to match the parallel graded step.

findings.step: Now the Primary bar in the 2020 group:
findings.why: This is a sentence fragment (no verb, just a trailing colon) and it drops the 'in % of the workforce' unit that the fully-worded step immediately above it supplied. A student has to guess both what's being asked for and what unit to answer in.
findings.fix: "Now read the Primary bar in the 2020 group. Its height, in % of the workforce, is"

findings.step: Nigeria's projected 2050 bar reads
findings.why: The parallel step directly above it states the unit ('Nigeria's 2020 bar, in millions, reads'); this one drops 'in millions'. The unit is inferable from the previous line, but the inconsistency is unnecessary and a careful reader may pause on it.

findings.step: P lies south of the 8°C line, so P is warmer than 8. Type the lowest whole temperature P could be, in °C.
findings.why: The sentence states P is strictly warmer than 8, then asks for 'the lowest whole temperature P could be' and expects the answer to be 8 itself. Read literally, the lowest whole number strictly greater than 8 is 9 — a careful student following the stated inequality is likely to answer 9 and be marked wrong.
findings.fix: Reword to avoid the contradiction, e.g. "P is warmer than 8°C, so treat 8°C as your boundary estimate for P. Type that boundary value, in °C."

findings.step: Type the largest total, in £, those 80 lower-earning households could contribute.
findings.why: Every other step in this walk states the operation to perform (divide, multiply, subtract). This step jumps straight to a result (2,000,000) without ever telling the student to multiply 80 by the £25,000 ceiling — they aren't told how to get the number, only what the number represents.
findings.fix: "80 households × the most any one of them could earn (£25,000) ="

findings.step: Type the smallest total, in £, the remaining 20 households must contribute.
findings.why: Same gap as the step above — it never says to subtract the previous total from the area's implied total income (£4,500,000) to get this figure.
findings.fix: "Subtract that from the area's total income (£4,500,000) to get what the remaining 20 households must contribute:"

findings.step: If no red arrowhead lands on London, how many red arrows must instead begin at London?
findings.why: This presumes every red arrow on the map connects to London (starts or ends there) — a fact never stated anywhere in the walk. A careful student could reasonably object that the red arrows might run between two other cities entirely.
findings.fix: Add a line establishing the map's scope before this step, e.g. "All the arrows drawn on this map run to or from London."

findings.step: The Leeds arrow is half as wide. Flow widths scale straight, so halve that value.
findings.why: 'Scale straight' is not standard phrasing for a 15-year-old and doesn't clearly mean 'directly proportional' on first read.
findings.fix: "Flow widths are directly proportional to the number of people, so halve that value."

findings.step: Type the position of the economic option, counting 1 down to 4.
findings.why: Every other 'counting 1 ... down to 4 ...' instruction in this pack names what options 1 and 4 actually are (e.g. 'counting 1 for towards London down to 4 for commuter journeys'). This one just says '1 down to 4' with no anchor, breaking the pattern the student has been trained to rely on.
findings.fix: "counting 1 for weather down to 4 for universities"

findings.step: How many times bigger does the drawing look than the data really is? Divide the area factor by the data factor, to the nearest whole number.
findings.why: 'The area factor' and 'the data factor' are never introduced under those names in the two steps that actually computed them (100 and 29) — the student has to guess which earlier number each label refers back to.
findings.fix: Name the values when they're first computed, e.g. "...how many times the area does it have? (this is the area factor)" and "...divide London's population by Newcastle's (this is the data factor)", then this step can safely refer back to them by name.
